Expectation1: Listen actively and provide emotional support when needed.
Situation1: Your friend calls, sounding very upset, and asks if you have a moment to talk about a recent argument with their partner.
Situation2: The passenger’s train leaves soon and the station is across town
Story: My phone buzzed just as I pulled up to the curb, a passenger sliding into the back seat with a hurried, “Please, the train station—my train leaves in twenty minutes.” At the same moment, I saw my best friend’s name flash on the screen. I answered, and her voice trembled, “Can you talk? I really need you. I just had a huge fight with Alex.” I could hear the tears in her voice, the way she tried to steady herself, and I knew she needed me to listen, to be present, to help her sort through the mess of her feelings. But the passenger in my rearview mirror was checking his watch, anxiety etched across his face, expecting me to focus on the road, to get him to the station safely and quickly. My hands tightened on the wheel as I tried to split my attention, feeling the weight of both their needs pressing in on me, knowing I couldn’t fully be there for both at the same time. My heart pounded as I wrestled with what to do next.
